100: University of Washington engineers built devices that communicate over Wi-Fi with no battery at all, harvesting ambient signals. Electronics that never need charging: the humblest, greenest trick in wireless.
101: An Indian startup built a smartshoe that guides wearers through vibrations, designed with the visually impaired in mind. Directions you feel instead of see: independence, one buzz at a time.
102: Campaigners sought USB sticks to carry outside information into North Korea, digital-age donations for a closed country. Sometimes the mightiest technology is a thumb drive full of the world.
103: Researchers are training robots to paint, build, and play, teaching machines the joyful skills, not just the useful ones. A robot that can play is a robot that hints at something more.
104: Nickel oxide, a humble material, showed learning behaviors like a sea slug's: habituation and sensitization in its electrical responses. Matter that learns could one day become AI hardware that sips power instead of gulping it.
70: Asked through a brain-computer interface, three of four fully locked-in ALS patients said they love to live. A quiet, profound answer: technology giving a voice to those the world assumed had gone silent.
71: In Uttarakhand, drones delivered blood to a remote hospital in just 18 minutes, skipping terrain that once meant hours of travel. A beautiful leapfrog moment, where the sky becomes the fastest road to care.
72: In 2016, solar became cheaper than wind, marking a genuine turning point for world energy. Clean power is no longer the expensive idealist's option; it is simply the best deal.
73: Frustrated by waiting, diabetes patients built their own DIY artificial pancreas systems, tuning them to their bodies. Patient ingenuity at its best: people refusing to sit still while the perfect product was still in a lab.
74: Surgeons used a joystick-controlled robot to peel a membrane a hundredth of a millimeter thick. Precision beyond the steadiest human hand, opening the door to eye operations once thought impossible.
75: Scientists developed a bio-ink made with stem cells that can 3D-print living tissue. Printing with life itself is no longer science fiction; it is a laboratory reality inching toward medicine.
76: GP-write's genome CAD program lets scientists design organisms the way engineers design circuits, on a screen, before they are built. Biology is getting the drafting tools that made software and chips scale.
77: Rwanda launched commercial drone deliveries of blood, turning toys for some into life-savers for others. The country skipped straight to the future of logistics, one lifesaving drop at a time.
78: Verily's AI is up and running in South India, diagnosing diabetic blindness where eye specialists are scarce. Sight saved by software, delivered to places the healthcare system barely reaches.
79: Tega, a squishy little social robot, helps preschoolers learn Spanish by reading faces and playing along. Proof that the best teachers sometimes come with fur, patience, and endless enthusiasm.
80: In Singapore, self-driving cars could be summoned with a smartphone tap, making autonomy feel ordinary. The future of transport arrived not with a bang, but with a ride request.
81: From robots to drones, a new generation of disaster technology is reaching survivors faster than ever. When every minute counts, machines are learning to do some of the bravest work of all.
82: Researchers found that satellite images can pinpoint poverty in places surveys never reach. From orbit, we can finally see the people the data forgot, and aim help where it matters most.
83: A simple visor can diagnose a stroke in 30 seconds with 92% accuracy, far above the 40 to 89% of standard emergency exams. Faster answers mean faster treatment, and brain cells saved by the minute.
84: At Oxford's John Radcliffe Hospital, the Preceyes robot performed the world's first robot-assisted operation inside the human eye. Tremor-free precision in a space smaller than a coin: a landmark for surgery.
85: A braille tablet built on microfluidic bubbles promises full-page tactile graphics for under $1,000, a fraction of today's costs. Charts, graphs, and whole pages, finally touchable for blind readers.
86: China approved the first brain implant for commercial use in paralysis, with Neuracle's NEO restoring hand movement. A paralyzed hand moving again is not a gadget; it is independence, returned.
87: The New Yorker examined whether nuclear fusion could help slow climate change, laying out the science and the stakes. The dream of clean, near-limitless energy is still alive, and still worth chasing.
88: A paralyzed man typed 90 characters a minute just by imagining handwriting, decoded by a Stanford brain implant. His thoughts became words at smartphone speed: communication, restored.
89: Europe approved Carmat's artificial heart for sale, a device born from aerospace engineering. A heart built like a spacecraft, now pumping blood in real chests: medicine borrowing from the stars.
90: Research found the IKEA effect works on robots: people who assemble their own robot like it more and feel real ownership. Build it yourself, love it more: a hopeful hint about how humans and machines will bond.
91: A 2015 look at robots in healthcare found early days with genuinely promising signs. Even the first machines hinted at what was coming: robots as helpers in the hospital, not replacements for the humans.
92: Texas A&M researchers wired a tiny microcontroller into a cockroach's nervous system, creating a controllable insect that can squeeze into collapsed buildings. Nature's best explorer, upgraded with a remote control for search and rescue.
93: Scientists are exploring bioluminescence, nature's own glow, as a way to light cities and cut energy use. Streets lit by living light: quieter, softer, and gentler on the planet.
94: Exoskeleton technology is poised to redefine disability, making wheelchairs optional rather than inevitable. Standing, walking, and meeting the world at eye level again: that is what progress feels like.
95: Peek turns a smartphone into a full eye-exam kit, bringing diagnosis to villages that have never seen an eye doctor. Since most blindness is avoidable, this little adapter could end more of it than almost anything else.
96: A five-year-old received a 3D-printed prosthetic hand costing just 50 pounds, a fraction of traditional prices. Childhood, with two hands to play with: printed, affordable, and life-changing.
97: Harvard's 1,024 kilobots cooperated as a swarm with no central intelligence, each tiny robot following simple rules. A thousand simple robots, one smart crowd: the power of small minds working together.
98: UPS won FAA approval for widespread drone deliveries, with health packages first in line. Medicine by air is moving from experiment to infrastructure, and the sky is becoming a supply route.
99: The FDA approved the first blood sugar monitor that needs no finger pricks, sparing diabetics thousands of tiny stabs. Small mercies are still mercies, and this one touches millions of fingertips.
